name: The AI Enablement Audit in Investment Firms
title: The AI Enablement Audit in Investment Firms
answer: The AI enablement audit in investment firms is a structured review of how artificial intelligence is actually used across research, trading, operations and client service, and whether that use is documented, controlled and defensible. It sits inside governance and fiduciary risk because an investment firm owes duties of care and loyalty to the people whose money it manages, and those duties do not change when a model is introduced. The audit covers the whole estate: vendor tools, in-house models, spreadsheets with embedded predictions, and the informal use of public chatbots by staff. Its output is a picture of what is enabled, who owns it, and where the evidence sits.

sections.body: The AI enablement audit in investment firms is a structured review of how artificial intelligence is actually used across research, trading, operations and client service, and whether that use is documented, controlled and defensible. It sits inside governance and fiduciary risk because an investment firm owes duties of care and loyalty to the people whose money it manages, and those duties do not change when a model is introduced. The audit covers the whole estate: vendor tools, in-house models, spreadsheets with embedded predictions, and the informal use of public chatbots by staff. Its output is a picture of what is enabled, who owns it, and where the evidence sits.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: What the audit runs on is rarely a single system. It draws on model inventories, procurement records, access logs, vendor due diligence files, incident tickets and the policies that govern research and trading. In most firms the raw material is scattered across a compliance platform, a data catalogue, an identity provider and the desks themselves, which is why the first pass is usually an inventory rather than a test. The audit also depends on people: a named owner for each tool, a control function able to read the output, and a record of who approved the use and when. Where a firm tracks many instruments and counterparties, the same registers that hold positions and filings often become the spine of the audit.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The work is done in stages, and the sequence matters more than the sophistication of any single step. A firm starts by listing every AI-enabled process and the decision it touches, then classifies each by materiality and by whether a human can meaningfully review the output. Evidence is gathered against a control framework, tested on a sample basis, and where a gap appears it is logged with an owner and a date. Interviews with desk heads and control staff usually reveal more than the documentation does, because informal use is the hardest part to see. Findings are then written up so that a board or an investment committee can read them without a technical translator.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights, risk and provenance turn on three questions: whose data went in, who is accountable for what came out, and whether the firm can reproduce the result later. Vendor contracts need to address training on firm data, retention, subprocessors and the right to audit, and the firm needs a lawful basis for any personal data involved. Provenance matters for advice and for records, since a recommendation that cannot be traced to its inputs is difficult to defend to a client, a regulator or a court. The audit should also test whether disclosures to clients are accurate about how AI is used, and whether staff understand that the model does not absorb their responsibility. Where the firm relies on a third party, the accountability stays with the firm.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Expect the audit to move from a periodic project to a standing control, refreshed as tools change and as expectations from regulators and clients tighten. Model inventories will increasingly be linked to live monitoring, so that drift, outages and unexpected behaviour surface before a client does. Firms that treat the audit as evidence gathering rather than a compliance ritual will find it useful in procurement, in disputes and in explaining decisions to a board. The open questions are how to evidence human oversight when review is nominal, and how to keep pace with tools that are adopted faster than any policy cycle. The direction is toward traceability as a default rather than an afterthought.
